dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Contoso plans to deploy a new Azure container registry. The registry must replicate its images to three Azure regions from a single login server, and it must be reachable only through a private endpoint in a virtual network. Which pricing plan must you select when you create the registry?
spiegazione: Correct: Premium. The Azure Container Registry SKU feature matrix lists both geo-replication and private link with private endpoints as supported only in the Premium plan. A single Premium registry replicated to several regions still exposes one global login server (myregistry.azurecr.io), which is exactly what the scenario requires. Basic is wrong: it is the cost-optimized entry point for developers and supports neither geo-replication nor private endpoints. Standard is wrong: it raises included storage and image throughput over Basic but the SKU table marks geo-replication and private link as N/A for Standard. 'Standard with zone redundancy enabled' is wrong because it confuses two different capabilities: zone redundancy protects against a zonal outage inside one region and is supported on all three plans, so enabling it does not add geo-replication or private endpoint support to a Standard registry.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A colleague is reviewing the Access keys blade of an Azure container registry and asks you about the admin user account. Which statement accurately describes the admin user account of an Azure container registry?
opzione_a: The admin account is enabled by default on every new registry.
opzione_b: The admin account provides two passwords, and either password can be used with the docker login command.
opzione_c: You can assign the AcrPull role to the admin account so that it is limited to pull-only access.
opzione_d: The admin account issues a separate credential set for each user who signs in to the registry.
spiegazione: Correct: the admin account has two passwords, both of which can be regenerated, and you can pass the admin username with either password to docker login. Having two passwords lets you keep connectivity through one password while you rotate the other. Option a is wrong: Microsoft Learn states that each container registry includes an admin user account that is disabled by default; you must explicitly enable it (for example, az acr update -n <acrName> --admin-enabled true, or the Admin user check box under Settings > Access keys). Option c is wrong: the admin account is not integrated with Microsoft Entra ID and therefore has no Azure RBAC role assignments - the authentication options table shows 'No, always pull and push access' for it, so it can never be reduced to pull-only. Option d is wrong: there is a single admin account per registry and it is designed for a single user, mainly for testing; all users who authenticate with it appear as the same identity, which is why Microsoft advises against sharing it among multiple users.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A Linux virtual machine named vm1 runs a containerized workload and has a system-assigned managed identity. The identity must be able to pull container images from a registry named acr1, but it must not be able to push images, delete images, or change the registry configuration. The registry uses the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. You must apply the principle of least privilege. Which role should you assign, and at which scope?
opzione_d: AcrPull, scoped to the subscription that contains acr1
spiegazione: Correct: AcrPull scoped to acr1. For registries in the RBAC Registry Permissions mode, Microsoft Learn recommends AcrPull for identities that only need to pull images and artifacts; it grants data plane read-only access with no control plane or write permissions. Assigning it directly on the registry resource limits the identity to exactly one registry. Option b is wrong: Reader is a control plane role that lets you view the registry resource and its configuration, but it grants no data plane permission, so docker pull still fails. Option c is wrong: AcrPush grants push in addition to pull, which exceeds what the workload needs and violates least privilege. Option d is wrong for the scope, not the role: assigning AcrPull at the subscription lets the VM pull from every registry in that subscription now and in the future, which is broader than required. Azure RBAC assignments are inherited downward, so the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement is the registry itself.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A build server has the Azure CLI installed but has no Docker Engine and cannot run Docker commands. You must copy the multi-architecture nginx:latest image from Docker Hub into an Azure container registry named acrprod, and every architecture listed in the image manifest list must be copied. Which command should you run?
opzione_b: az acr import --name acrprod --source docker.io/library/nginx:latest --image nginx:v1
opzione_c: docker pull nginx:latest, then docker tag and docker push acrprod.azurecr.io/nginx:v1
opzione_d: az acr repository show --name acrprod --repository nginx
spiegazione: Correct: az acr import copies images into a registry by using Azure APIs without any Docker commands, so no local Docker installation is needed, and Microsoft Learn states that when you import a multi-architecture image such as an official Docker image, images for all architectures and platforms specified in the manifest list are copied. Because hello-world and nginx are official Docker Hub images, the source path includes the default library repository, as in docker.io/library/nginx:latest. Option a is wrong: az acr build runs a quick task that builds an image from a Dockerfile and a source context - it is for building, not for copying an existing image from another registry. Option c is wrong: it is the classic pull/tag/push workaround, which requires a working Docker Engine that the build server does not have, and a plain docker pull retrieves only the single architecture matching the client platform rather than the whole manifest list. Option d is wrong: az acr repository show only displays the attributes of a repository that already exists in the registry; it copies nothing.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Your team maintains several application images that are built FROM a common base image stored in the same Azure container registry. Whenever the base image is patched and pushed again, every dependent application image must be rebuilt automatically, with no manual command and no dependency on a developer workstation. What should you configure?
opzione_a: An Azure Container Registry task that uses a base image update trigger
opzione_b: A registry webhook that calls an Azure function, which then runs docker build on a virtual machine
opzione_c: A quick task that is started with az acr build each time the base image changes
opzione_d: An Azure Container Registry task that uses a timer trigger scheduled to run every night
spiegazione: Correct: ACR Tasks can track an application image's dependency on a base image at build time. When the updated base image is pushed to your registry, or updated in a public repo such as Docker Hub, the task automatically rebuilds any application image based on it - this is the documented way to automate OS and framework patching without manually tracking every dependent image. Option b is wrong: it is an unnecessary custom solution that reintroduces a build host to maintain and duplicates a capability ACR Tasks already provides natively. Option c is wrong: a quick task (az acr build) is an on-demand, manually invoked build for the inner-loop development cycle; something or someone still has to notice the base image changed and run the command, which the requirement forbids. Option d is wrong: a timer trigger runs the task on a fixed schedule regardless of whether the base image changed, so rebuilds are delayed until the next scheduled run and happen even when nothing was patched - it does not react to the base image update itself.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: An existing Azure container registry named acr1 uses the Premium pricing plan and is geo-replicated to the West Europe and East US regions. The registry stores 60 GiB of images. To reduce cost, you open Settings > Properties in the Azure portal and try to change the pricing plan to Standard, but the operation fails. What should you do first?
opzione_a: Delete the geo-replicas in West Europe and East US, and then change the pricing plan.
opzione_b: Disable the admin user account on acr1, and then change the pricing plan.
opzione_c: Reduce the registry's storage consumption below the 100 GiB that is included with the Standard plan.
opzione_d: Delete acr1 and recreate it with the Standard plan, because a registry's pricing plan cannot be changed after creation.
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn states that when you move from Premium to a lower plan, features specific to Premium are disabled, and in some cases you must remove the related resources first - you must delete any geo-replications or connected registries before you can switch from Premium to Standard or Basic. Geo-replication is a Premium-only feature, so the replicas block the downgrade. Option b is wrong: the admin account is available in every plan and is unrelated to changing the pricing plan. Option c is wrong on two counts: 100 GiB is the storage included in the Standard daily rate, not a cap - additional storage is simply billed per GiB up to the plan's storage limit, and the Standard storage limit is 40 TiB, so 60 GiB is nowhere near a blocker. Option d is wrong: a registry's plan can be changed at any time in the portal, with az acr update --sku, or with Update-AzContainerRegistry, and the change causes no downtime or impact on registry operations.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: An Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster named aks1 must pull container images from an existing registry named acrshared, which uses the Basic plan and the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. The solution must not require an image pull secret in the cluster and must grant the smallest set of permissions possible. What should you do?
opzione_a: Run az aks update --name aks1 --resource-group rg1 --attach-acr acrshared.
opzione_b: Enable the admin user on acrshared and create a Kubernetes secret from the admin username and password.
opzione_c: Assign the AcrPush role to the kubelet managed identity of aks1 on acrshared.
opzione_d: Assign the Reader role to the control plane managed identity of aks1 on acrshared.
spiegazione: Correct: az aks update --attach-acr configures the AKS-to-ACR integration, which assigns the AcrPull role to the Microsoft Entra managed identity associated with the cluster's agent pool (the kubelet identity). Microsoft Learn presents this as the automatic authentication mechanism between AKS and ACR, so no image pull secret is needed, and AcrPull is pull-only. Any ACR plan works - the article's own example creates the registry with --sku basic. Option b is wrong: it uses the shared admin account in an image pull secret, which is the credential-based approach Microsoft explicitly steers away from (image pull secrets are for private external registries), and the admin account always carries push and pull access. Option c is wrong in the role, not the identity: AcrPush would work for pulling but grants push as well, exceeding least privilege. Option d is wrong on both counts: images are pulled by the kubelet identity, not the control plane identity, and Reader is a control plane role that grants no data plane pull permission.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are documenting which Azure Container Registry capabilities justify the cost of the Premium pricing plan for your organization. Which three features are available only in the Premium plan? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
spiegazione: Correct: geo-replication, content trust, and customer-managed keys are all marked Supported for Premium only and N/A for Basic and Standard in the Azure Container Registry SKU features and limits table. Geo-replication gives high availability by managing a single registry across multiple regions; content trust implements the Docker Content Trust model for pushing and pulling signed images; customer-managed keys let you encrypt registry content with your own key. Option d is wrong: the SKU table lists availability zones as Supported for Basic, Standard, and Premium, and the article states that all SKUs have zone redundancy enabled by default in supported regions - it is not a Premium differentiator. Option e is wrong: anonymous pull access is N/A for Basic but Supported for both Standard and Premium, so it is not Premium-only. Other genuinely Premium-only capabilities not listed here include private link with private endpoints, dedicated data endpoints, connected registries, retention policy for untagged manifests, and dedicated agent pools for Tasks.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are planning automated image builds by using Azure Container Registry tasks. Which three events can automatically trigger a task run? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: A commit to a GitHub repository that is configured as the task's source code context
opzione_b: An update to the base image that the task's image is built from
opzione_c: A timer schedule defined on the task
opzione_d: A docker pull of an image from the registry
opzione_e: A change to the registry's pricing plan
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft Learn describes exactly these three categories of automatically triggered tasks. Source code update triggers fire when code is committed, or a pull request is made or updated, in a public or private Git repository in GitHub or Azure DevOps (the commit trigger is enabled by default; the pull request trigger is not). Base image update triggers rebuild application images when their base image is pushed to your registry or updated in a public repo such as Docker Hub. Timer triggers run a task on a defined schedule. Option d is wrong: pulling an image is a data plane read operation - it can raise a registry webhook event to notify an external service, but it is not a task trigger. Option e is wrong: changing the pricing plan is a control plane configuration change; it causes no downtime and does not start a task run. Note that source code triggers require a personal access token so the task can create the webhook in the Git repo.
tags: acr,acr tasks,triggers,commit trigger,base image update,timer trigger

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: Registry acr1 must be reachable only from a virtual network named vnet1. You plan to create a private endpoint for acr1 in vnet1, integrate it with a private DNS zone so that clients keep using the acr1.azurecr.io name, and then set Public network access to Disabled on the Networking blade. Your CI pipeline currently runs az acr build against acr1 from a hosted agent on the internet. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Minimum pricing plan required for the private endpoint: [Basic | Standard | Premium]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone that must resolve the registry FQDN: [privatelink.azurecr.io | privatelink.registry.azure.com | acr.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_c: Effect on az acr build from the hosted agent after public network access is disabled: [It continues to work unchanged | It fails unless you use a dedicated agent pool or allow the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPs | It works only if the admin user is enabled]
risposta_corretta: Premium,privatelink.azurecr.io,It fails unless you use a dedicated agent pool or allow the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPs
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Premium: private link with private endpoints is available in the Premium container registry service tier, with a maximum of 200 private endpoints. Basic and Standard are marked N/A for private link in the SKU feature matrix. Dropdown 2 - privatelink.azurecr.io: to override the default DNS resolution for an Azure container registry with a private zone, the zone must be named privatelink.azurecr.io; the portal likewise offers (New) privatelink.azurecr.io during private endpoint creation. The other two names are invented and would never be queried, because the registry FQDN resolves through a CNAME to <registry>.privatelink.azurecr.io. Dropdown 3 - it fails: Microsoft Learn explicitly notes that if you disable public network access, az acr build commands no longer work, because Tasks reserve a set of public IPs in each region for outbound requests. The documented options are to assign a dedicated agent pool (a Premium feature) or to add the regional AzureContainerRegistry service tag IPv4 ranges to the firewall access rules. 'Continues to work unchanged' contradicts the documentation, and enabling the admin user changes only authentication, not network reachability. Note that creating a private endpoint also automatically enables dedicated data endpoints, so plan for one private IP for the global endpoint plus one per geo-replica for the data endpoints.
tags: acr,private endpoint,private link,privatelink.azurecr.io,public network access,az acr build

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: You are sizing Azure container registries for several teams and need to compare the plans. Select the correct value for each statement based on the Azure Container Registry service tier features and limits.
opzione_a: Storage included in the daily rate for a Standard registry: [10 GiB | 100 GiB | 500 GiB]
opzione_b: Maximum number of webhooks for a Basic registry: [2 | 10 | 500]
opzione_c: Storage limit for a Premium registry: [40 TiB | 100 TiB | 500 TiB]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 100 GiB: the SKU features and limits table lists included storage as 10 GiB for Basic, 100 GiB for Standard, and 500 GiB for Premium. This is the storage included in the daily rate; you can use additional storage up to the plan's storage limit at an extra daily per-GiB rate, so 10 GiB (Basic) and 500 GiB (Premium) are the values for the other two plans. Dropdown 2 - 2: the webhook limit is 2 for Basic, 10 for Standard, and 500 for Premium, so 10 and 500 belong to the other plans. Dropdown 3 - 100 TiB: the storage limit is 40 TiB for both Basic and Standard and 100 TiB for Premium; 40 TiB is the Basic/Standard limit, and 500 TiB does not appear in the table at all (500 GiB is Premium's included storage, which is a different figure). You can check a registry's current consumption against these limits on the registry Overview page in the portal, or with az acr show-usage.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda: A Docker-enabled Linux virtual machine named vm1 is configured with a user-assigned managed identity named id1. The VM must pull images from a registry named acr1 without any credentials being stored on the VM. The registry uses the RBAC Registry Permissions role assignment mode. Select the appropriate option to complete each step.
opzione_a: Role to assign to id1, scoped to acr1: [AcrPull | AcrPush | Contributor]
opzione_b: Command to run on vm1 to sign in to the Azure CLI: [az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID> | az login --service-principal --username <appId> --password <secret> | az acr credential show --name acr1]
opzione_c: Command to run next on vm1 to authenticate to the registry: [az acr login --name acr1 | az acr update --name acr1 --admin-enabled true | az acr token create --name acr1 --repository nginx content/read]
risposta_corretta: AcrPull,az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID>,az acr login --name acr1
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - AcrPull: for a non-ABAC registry, the managed identity article says to assign AcrPull, which provides pull permissions only, scoped to the registry resource ID. AcrPush would additionally allow pushing, and Contributor is a control plane role that would let the identity reconfigure or delete the registry - both exceed what a pull-only workload needs. Dropdown 2 - az login --identity --username <id1 resource ID>: this is the documented way to sign the Azure CLI in with a user-assigned managed identity on the VM (a system-assigned identity would use az login --identity with no username). az login --service-principal requires a secret to be stored on the VM, which the requirement forbids, and az acr credential show retrieves the admin account credentials - also a stored credential, and it does not sign anyone in. Dropdown 3 - az acr login --name acr1: after az login, the CLI reuses the Microsoft Entra token it created to authenticate the session with the registry, and subsequent docker pull commands need no credentials. Keep in mind the token az acr login uses is valid for 3 hours. az acr update --admin-enabled true enables the admin account, which is the credential-based approach being avoided, and az acr token create creates a non-Microsoft Entra repository-scoped token, which again means managing a secret.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda:
A registry named acr1 uses the Standard pricing plan, and its admin user account is currently enabled. All developers share the admin credentials to run docker login. Your team is reviewing how clients authenticate to acr1. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. Disabling the admin account and having developers authenticate with az acr login means their registry access is governed by Azure RBAC role assignments.
2. The Microsoft Entra token that az acr login places in the Docker configuration file remains valid for 30 days.
3. Anonymous pull access can be enabled on acr1 without changing the registry's pricing plan.
opzione_a: Disabling the admin account and having developers authenticate with az acr login means their registry access is governed by Azure RBAC role assignments.
opzione_b: The Microsoft Entra token that az acr login places in the Docker configuration file remains valid for 30 days.
opzione_c: Anonymous pull access can be enabled on acr1 without changing the registry's pricing plan.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: the authentication options table shows that individual Microsoft Entra identity sign-in via az acr login supports Azure RBAC, whereas the admin user row shows 'No, always pull and push access'. Using az acr login with Azure identities enables Azure role-based access control, so each developer can be granted only the roles they need (for example AcrPull or AcrPush). This is why Microsoft recommends individual identities for users and service principals or managed identities for headless scenarios instead of the shared admin account. Statement 2 - No: Microsoft Learn states that for registry access, the token that az acr login uses is valid for 3 hours, so you should always sign in to the registry before running a docker command and re-run az acr login to refresh an expired token. 30 days is not a documented ACR token lifetime (1 year is the default expiry of a service principal password, which is a different thing). Statement 3 - Yes: the SKU features and limits table marks anonymous pull access as N/A for Basic but Supported for both Standard and Premium. Because acr1 already uses Standard, the feature can be turned on with no plan change. Note that this statement is about technical feasibility, not about whether anonymous pull is advisable for a private registry.
tags: acr,authentication,admin account,az acr login,token lifetime,anonymous pull

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Create and manage an Azure container registry
domanda:
From Azure Cloud Shell, you must copy container images into a registry named acrprod by using az acr import. The sources include a public registry, an Azure container registry in another Microsoft Entra tenant, and an Azure container registry in your own tenant that has public network access disabled. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. A local Docker Engine installation is required for az acr import to copy the images.
2. You can import an image from an Azure container registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant by specifying the source registry's login server name together with credentials that allow pull access to it.
3. To import from a source Azure container registry that has public network access disabled, you specify the source registry by its resource ID with the --registry parameter.
opzione_a: A local Docker Engine installation is required for az acr import to copy the images.
opzione_b: You can import an image from an Azure container registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant by specifying the source registry's login server name together with credentials that allow pull access to it.
opzione_c: To import from a source Azure container registry that has public network access disabled, you specify the source registry by its resource ID with the --registry parameter.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: importing images to an Azure container registry is done through Azure APIs without using Docker commands. Microsoft Learn lists as a benefit that if your client environment doesn't need a local Docker installation, you can import any container image regardless of the supported OS type - which is precisely why the command works from Azure Cloud Shell. Statement 2 - Yes: to import images from a registry in a different Microsoft Entra tenant, you specify the source registry by login server name and provide credentials that enable pull access, for example the appId and password of a service principal that has AcrPull (or Container Registry Repository Reader on an ABAC-enabled registry) on the source, a non-Microsoft Entra repository-scoped token, or an access token passed as the password. Be aware that cross-tenant import isn't supported over a public-access-disabled registry. Statement 3 - Yes: when public access to the source registry is disabled, you supply the resource ID of the source registry with the --registry parameter and the --source parameter then specifies only the repository and tag, not the login server name. Also remember that a network-restricted registry must allow access by trusted services to bypass the network, otherwise the import fails; that setting is enabled by default.
tags: acr,az acr import,cross-tenant,resource id,trusted services,cloud shell
